# Abstract

\noindent MixMustR is a novel Bayesian mixture model package designed to estimate source mixing proportions in complex ecological systems. Traditional mixture models, often limited by the number of tracers and predefined sources, struggle with infinite solutions and possibly unsampled sources. MixMustR addresses these challenges by leveraging two independent data streams: chemical tracers (e.g., stable isotopes, fatty acids) and source composition data (e.g., from environmental DNA metabarcoding). Written in R and utilising the Stan language for probabilistic programming, MixMustR incorporates uncertainty in input data and allows for the estimation of an additional unsampled source component. The package offers eight model variants, enabling flexibility in error structures, unsampled source estimation, and hierarchical grouping. Performance testing with synthetic datasets demonstrates MixMustR's ability to recover original mixing proportions. MixMustR has broad applicability in ecological research, particularly in studies integrating multiple tracers to unravel source-sink dynamics and trophic interactions. A full tutorial is available on GitHub.

# Introduction

\noindent Mixture or mixing models (used synonymously in this paper) provide a flexible statistical framework for analysing complex datasets in which observations arise from multiple underlying sources or groups with distinct characteristics [@robert1999; @mclachlan2019anrevstat]. Mixture models have been widely applied to identify the contribution of different sources to mixtures, such as in trophic ecology where the goal is to estimate the dietary contributions of different food sources to consumer tissues [@phillips2012jmamm; @phillips2014canzoo; @stock2018]. Estimating the sources of organic carbon within soil samples has also seen an application of increasingly complex mixture models to identify the major drivers of carbon sequestration in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems (e.g., refs. [@reef2017aslo; @ortega2020aslo; @erlania2023scitot; @erlania2024ecolind]). These mixture models typically rely on chemical tracers (often stable isotopes $\delta$^13^C and $\delta$^15^N, and/or total C:N) from plant sources that capture carbon through photosynthesis.

Traditional approaches to solving the mixture problem used linear models to estimate proportions for two sources using a single stable isotope (typically $\delta$^13^C) with the assumption of no variability within sources [@phillips2001]. This approach was later extended in the "IsoError" model to include variability within sources [@phillips2001]. However, only a limited number of sources can be considered in these models because they cannot deterministically solve mass-balance equations when the number of sources exceeds the number of tracers plus one. However, complex ecological systems often have many more sources than the number of available tracers within a particular tracer group (e.g., stable isotopes). For example, in a diverse landscape, there may be dozens of potential autotrophic sources contributing to the organic carbon buried within a soil sink. Early attempts to solve this "underdetermined" problem of the unsampled sources involved an iterative algorithm to produce a range of feasible solutions based on investigator-defined thresholds (e.g., IsoSource [@phillips2003; @parnell2010]), though these did not provide any quantification as to which solutions were most likely.

More recently, Bayesian mixture models have allowed for the incorporation of uncertainty in input data at different levels and the estimation of uncertainty of source mixing proportions [@moore2008; @parnell2010; @parnell2013; @neubauer2013; @neubauer2015; @stock2018]. Early models such as MixSIR introduced Bayesian inference into isotope mixture models [@moore2008], and were later refined by SIAR (Stable Isotope Analysis in R [@parnell2010]) to handle larger datasets and additional uncertainty parameters. MixSIAR further expanded these capabilities by incorporating covariates and hierarchical structures [@stock2018], making it adaptable to complex ecological systems. More recent advancements, such as the two-trophic-level MixSIAR [@heikkinen2022], extend the framework to account for multiple trophic steps, thereby improving the depth of ecological inference by better capturing some structural complexity of food webs. While these models differ in computational complexity and assumptions, they collectively advanced the application of mixture models in ecological research and provide increasingly reliable insights into ecosystem source-sink dynamics.

Recent studies dealing with complex mixtures have explored multiple tracers, such as stable isotopes alongside fatty acids to better understand the source contributions [@neubauer2015; @hoenig2022]. More recently, we have also seen applications of environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding to help unravel complex mixtures where there may be overlap in isotopic tracer signatures (e.g., [@reef2017aslo; @ortega2020aslo]). However, these explorations have typically been independent to the mixture model. Without an integrated model for multi-tracer analyses, the interpretation of these results has typically been limited to an ad-hoc, side-by-side comparison of tracer-specific outputs. To address this issue, mixture models have been produced for use in trophic studies, combining fatty acids/amino acids and stable isotopes data to enhance dietary estimations [@neubauer2015; @pickett2024]. However, although combining multiple tracers increases the discriminatory power of mixture models, it also introduces methodological challenges, such as differences in temporal integration and tracer-specific biases (e.g., different degradation rates [@nielsen2018]). These findings underscore the importance of selecting appropriate tracers based on study objectives and ecological context, as well as the need for methodological advancements to better integrate diverse biotracer data into ecological modelling.

Although mixture models typically focus on a predefined number of potential sources, in many real-world scenarios a portion of the mixture will originate from sources that are unable to be adequately sampled to obtain a representative signature. By the latter we mean one that incorporates the major temporal axes of variation alongside the potential spatial domain over which a contribution can be made to the mixture of interest. The application of mixture models becomes non-trivial when the number of source components is unknown because, if no external information is available, an infinite set of mixtures can generate the same observation, so estimating the true number of mixture components is indeed impossible [@richardson1997statsmet; @robert1999; @phillips2001; @phillips2003; @neubauer2013]. At the same time, ignoring the possibility that not all potential sources have been sampled may produce spurious conclusions because most mixture models assume that source mixing contributions sum to unity [@stock2018]. An alternative is to recognize this uncertainty, and seek to determine the contribution of sources for which there is relatively high confidence in obtaining a representative tracer signature, and allowing for other source contributions to be part of the final mixture model solution (e.g., as a probability mass that was not attributable to the empirically sampled sources).

Here we introduce MixMustR, a flexible Bayesian mixture model package written in R [@r]. MixMustR writes models in the probabilistic programming language Stan [@rstan] to estimate source mixing proportions. It does so by incorporating simultaneous likelihood evaluation from two independent data streams collected from the mixture of interest (Fig \ref{fig-1} a--b): one obtained from chemical tracers/biomarkers (i.e., a single tracer measurement per observation, e.g., from stable isotopes and fatty acids), and another yielding source composition (e.g., based on eDNA metabarcoding). MixMustR also allows for the estimation of an additional, unsampled source component. We evaluate the ability of MixMustR models to recover original source mixing proportions using two synthetic mixture datasets anchored to empirical values for a range of plant carbon sources in marine soils. Some of our model choices build on the widely-used MixSIAR [@stock2018], and we therefore explore how the two modelling approaches compare. A full tutorial on how to use MixMustR is available on GitHub (https://github.com/open-AIMS/MixMustR). We expect MixMustR to have wide applicability in ecological studies, particularly given the growing usage and availability of multiple tracers spanning traditional stable isotopes, fatty acids and eDNA metabarcoding to understand carbon source-sink dynamics [@reef2017aslo; @ortega2020aslo; @queiros2019ecolmonogr], and trophic interactions (e.g., refs. [@nielsen2018; @hoenig2022; @parravicini2020]).

# Methods

\noindent Many existing implementations of Bayesian mixture models use the Dirichlet distribution, $\mathcal{D}$, to estimate the contributing mixing proportion of each source to the final mixture [@robert1999]:

$$
\symbf{\pi} \sim \mathcal{D}(\symbf{\alpha}),
$$

\noindent with $\symbf{\pi}$ being a vector of $J$ elements, each representing a mixing proportion for the $j^{\text{th}}$ source, so that $\sum_{j=1}^{J}\pi_j = 1$. The mixing proportions are estimated from the prior concentration parameter vector, $\symbf{\alpha}$, which often come in the form of a user-informed prior, and a normal likelihood

$$
Y \sim \sum_{j=1}^{J} \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\theta_j, \sigma_j^2),
$$

\noindent with $Y$ being the mixture observation, $\theta_j$ and $\sigma_j^2$ being the mean signature (e.g., stable isotope) and variance associated with source $j$. Given the 0-1 bounded nature of the source-specific probabilities, and the fact that they must sum to one and are therefore interdependent [@stock2018], mixture models often adopt re-parametrisations of the Dirichlet such as the additive log-ratio which removes the above constraints in the parameter space, allowing the use of unconstrained (e.g., Gaussian) priors [@aitchison1999; @neubauer2015; @stock2018]. One disadvantage of the additive log-ratio is that it requires the arbitrary declaration of a source-reference probability to unconstrain the remaining set of estimable probabilities. MixMustR uses an alternative re-parametrisation of the Dirichlet which does not require such declaration. This is achieved via the softmax function ($\vartheta$) in Stan:

$$
\symbf{\pi} = \vartheta(\symbf{\zeta}) = \frac{e^{\symbf{\zeta}}}{\sum e^{\symbf{\zeta}}},
$$

\noindent where $\symbf{\zeta}$ is an input vector of $J$ real elements, and $\pi_j$ is interpreted as the proportion that source $j$ contributes to the final mixture. Hence, rather than estimating the vector $\symbf{\pi}$ directly using the Dirichlet distribution as above, we estimate $\symbf{\zeta}$, and then apply the softmax function to calculate $\symbf{\pi}$. This is numerically convenient because $\symbf{\zeta}$ is unconstrained, so it can be estimated assuming Gaussian prior distributions.

\noindent \underline{\textit{MixMustR model variants}}

MixMustR currently allows for eight model variants which result from three user-driven binary choices (Fig \ref{fig-1} c--e): 1) should the model only ingest the mean sampled-source tracer signatures (equivalent to "residual-only error" structure of MixSIAR [@stock2018]) or should it incorporate their uncertainty based on user-provided mean, variance and sample size information (equivalent to "process error" structure of MixSIAR, Fig \ref{fig-1}c); 2) should the unsampled-source tracer signatures be fixed at the mean across all sampled sources, or should they rather be estimated based on a prior informed by the mean and variance across the sampled tracer signatures? (Fig \ref{fig-1}d) and 3) should all observations be treated as independent or should the model include a hierarchical grouping structure? (Fig \ref{fig-1}e).

\noindent \underline{\textit{An independent likelihood evaluation}}

A key novelty in MixMustR when compared to existing packages and models is the existence of a second data stream whose likelihood is independently evaluated. Doing so allows for extra calibration of the estimates of $\symbf{\zeta}$ that would otherwise occur on the basis of tracer data only (Fig \ref{fig-1} a). This model addition is only possible when the user has access to an independently collected data stream that yields compositional mixing proportion (Fig \ref{fig-1} b). This type of data is becoming increasingly common, for example, in samples that are simultaneously processed for stable isotope and eDNA composition. In the particular case of (e)DNA metabarcoding data, multiple additional unsampled sources (i.e., which might have not been included in the original source sampling) can emerge, and in MixMustR these need to be amalgamated a priori as part of a single unsampled source. For tractability, MixMustR currently ignores any biases such as trophic discrimination, fractionation, diagenesis, or any other analogous loss processes that would yield differences in the mixing proportions from each data stream, and therefore it is agnostic to the quality assessment of the mixing proportions (though see below how input parameter $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ helps address this limitation).

Solving for a source-specific $\zeta_j$ leads to $\zeta_j = \text{ln}\pi_j + c$, with $\text{ln}\pi_j$ being a log-transformed mixing proportion, and $c$ is an unknown constant which can be ignored in practice (i.e., $\sum\vartheta(\symbf{\zeta}) = \sum\vartheta(\symbf{\zeta + c})$). MixMustR transforms the mixing proportions from data stream 2, $\text{ln}\symbf{\rho}$, prior to running the model:

$$
\text{ln}\rho_{n, j} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\zeta_{n,j}, \sigma_{\text{ln}\rho_{n, j}}^2\right),
$$
$$
\forall n = 1, \dots, N, \quad \forall j = 1, \dots, J + 1, \quad \forall k = 1, \dots, K.
$$

\noindent where the observation- and source-specific standard deviations of $\text{ln}\rho$, $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho_{n, j}}$, is a measurement error on the latent $\zeta_{n,j}$, and in practice can be interpreted as the degree of confidence a user has in each element of $\text{ln}\rho$. Importantly, MixMustR ingests that confidence at the *observation and source* level, and offers the user a visualisation function to empirically gauge the appropriate value for $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho_{n, j}}$. An appropriate degree of confidence via $\text{ln}\rho$ will be study-specific, and might require an independent protocol based on elicitation of expert knowledge (e.g., extraction quality control and taxonomic reach of primers in the case of eDNA metabarcoding).

An alternative approach might be to leverage $\text{ln}\symbf{\rho}$ and $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ as prior information on $\symbf{\pi}$, although MixMustR explicitly treats these as independent data, of the same level of relevance as the data from data stream 1. However, in the online supplementary information, we also show that treating data stream 2 as a prior rather than using a likelihood evaluation leads to similar outcomes.

\noindent \underline{\textit{Estimating the tracer signatures}}

In a dataset containing $N$ observations, $J$ *sampled* sources (i.e., those initially considered by the researcher), and $K$ chemical tracers/biomarkers, MixMustR estimates the mixing contribution (i.e., proportions) of each sampled source to the final observed mixture in two different ways depending on the user choice (Fig \ref{fig-1}c):

\begin{centering}
\noindent\begin{minipage}{.4\linewidth}
Residual-only error
\[
  Y_{n, k} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(x_{j, k}\pi_{n, j}, \sigma_k^2\right)\phantom{\sqrt{\omega_{j, k}^2}}
\]
\end{minipage}
\begin{minipage}{.4\linewidth}
Process error
\[
  Y_{n, k} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{j, k}\pi_{n, j}, \omega_{j, k}^2 \pi_{n, j}^2\right)
\]
\end{minipage}
\end{centering}

$$
\forall n = 1, \dots, N, \quad \forall j = 1, \dots, J, \quad \forall k = 1, \dots, K.
$$

\noindent In the residual-error only option, $x_{j, k}$ is the user-informed mean signature for the $j^{\text{th}}$ sampled source and $k^{\text{th}}$ tracer and $\sigma_k$ is the tracer-specific residual error. In the process error option, $\mu_{j, k}$ is the *estimated* tracer- and source-specific signature and $\sqrt{\omega_{j, k}^2 \pi_{n, j}^2}$ is the process error (see definitions of $\mu$ and $\omega$ in the online supplementary information). In both versions, $\pi_{n, j}$ is the estimated mixing proportion from observation $n$ and source $j$.

\noindent \underline{\textit{Estimating an unsampled tracer signature}}

As we argue in the introduction, the researcher may not know the full suite of sources that contribute to a mixture, and for resource or logistical constraints may end up selecting a subset of sources for which they can obtain tracer data. Therefore, should an *unsampled* component be present in the sink mixture, it could be composed of one or multiple sources (Fig \ref{fig-1}a--b). MixMustR attempts to estimate the proportion of unknown contributions as a pooled source estimate that might comprise a collective of multiple unsampled sources. We note that studies have attempted to estimate the number of sources based on the data, but that is also a very challenging task (e.g., refs. [@robert1999; @neubauer2013]).

In MixSIAR, the presence of an unsampled source is indirectly captured by a multiplicative error term (parameter $\xi$ in ref. [@stock2018]) which MixMustR does not incorporate. Instead, MixMustR estimates an unsampled signature using two approaches: either by fixing or estimating the value of each unsampled tracer-specific signature. Fixing the unsampled signature values relies on either the mean tracer signature across all user-informed sampled sources signatures (i.e., for a given tracer $k$, the mean across all $x_j$), or the mean estimated signature (i.e., for a given tracer $k$, the mean across all $\mu_j$). Estimating the unsampled signature values relies on the same information, plus the pre-existing error structure. For example, assuming a process error model choice (see previous section), the unsampled signature could be estimated as:

$$
\bar{\mu}_{k} = \sum_{j=1}^{J} \mu_{j, k} / J
$$
$$
\bar{\omega}_{k} = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{J} \omega_{j, k}^2 / J}
$$

\smallskip

\begin{centering}
\noindent\begin{minipage}{.45\linewidth}
Fixing
\[
  \phantom{mu_{J + 1, k}}
\] \[
  Y_{n, k} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\bar{\mu}_{k} \pi_{n, J + 1}, \bar{\omega}_{k}^2 \pi_{n, J + 1}^2\right)
\]
\end{minipage}
\begin{minipage}{.45\linewidth}
Estimating value
\[
  \mu_{J + 1, k} \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{\mu}_{k}, \bar{\omega}_{k})
\] \[
  Y_{n, k} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu_{J + 1, k} \pi_{n, J + 1}, \bar{\omega}_{k}^2 \pi_{n, J + 1}^2\right)
\]
\end{minipage}
\end{centering}

$$
\forall n = 1, \dots, N \quad \forall k = 1, \dots, K.
$$

It is important to note here that in considering an additional unsampled source, $\sum_{j=1}^{J + 1}\pi_j = 1$.

\noindent \underline{\textit{Incorporating group-level structure}}

The final model choice MixMustR offers pertains to the possibility of imposing a group-level, hierarchical structure as part of the estimation process for $\symbf{\zeta}$ by assuming that each observation $n$ within a group $g$ emerges from a within group-mean, $\Delta_{g_{n, j}}$, and an overall residual error $\epsilon$:

$$
\zeta_{n, j} \sim \mathcal{N}(\Delta_{g_{n, j}}, \epsilon^2);
$$
$$
\Delta_{g_{n, j}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\Delta_{g_j}}^2);
$$
$$
\sigma_{\Delta_{g_j}} \sim \mathcal{N}^{\text{+}}(0, 1); \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}^{\text{+}}(0, 1).
$$
$$
\forall n = 1, \dots, N, \quad \forall j = 1, \dots, J + 1, \quad \forall k = 1, \dots, K.
$$

MixMustR creates the Stan code as part of the pipeline, and therefore the user can manually change the priors on $\epsilon$ and $\sigma_{\Delta_{g_j}}$ before running the model, where, $\mathcal{N}^{\text{+}}$ denotes the half-normal distribution.

\noindent \underline{\textit{Performance testing with synthetic data}}

We tested MixMustR's performance on two synthetic datasets that mimic the tracer signatures obtained from a collection of spatially discrete marine soil samples taken across a seascape, and six potential carbon sources that have typically been explored in blue carbon studies to date [@dahl2025oneearth; @macreadie2019natcommun]. These datasets are incorporated as part of the MixMustR package, and were simulated using eight tracers: six fatty acids (24:0, 18:1w9, 18:2w6, 18:3w3, 20:4w6, 20:5w3) and two stable isotopes ($\delta$(^13^C/^12^C), $\delta$(^15^N/^14^N)). The six organic carbon sources considered (the *sampled* sources) included: mangrove, saltmarsh, macroalgae, seagrass, terrestrial grass and plankton. Tracer values (mean and standard deviation) associated with each sampled source were taken from the published literature (Table S1). A total of 79 soil sample observations were simulated, organised into an unbalanced hierarchical grouping design of seven groups that mimicked a typical sampling design of different locations within a seascape (e.g., three mangrove stands, three seagrass beds, etc.), each containing between 4 to 26 independent soil samples. Individual synthetic soil sample mixture signatures were calculated by multiplying tracer values with source-specific mixing proportions (see @fig-2 for the resulting isospace). For simplicity, within a given source, different tracers were assumed to contribute equally (i.e., with the same mixing proportion) to the respective mixture signatures.

The contributions of the sampled sources do not sum to one, i.e., we deliberately simulated a dataset with *unsampled* sources in every observation. b) The isospace of sediment cores (each point and symbol matches a line in a), and the mean (+/- S.D.) isotopic signature of each sampled source. The mixing proportions were simulated in a hierarchical manner using the Dirichlet distribution. We first sampled seven group means of mixing proportions each for the six sampled sources using a generic $\symbf{\alpha}$. Then, using these group-level means as concentration parameters ($\alpha$), we generated the individual proportions within each of the seven groups, generating a 79 $\times$ 6 matrix of mixing proportions. We then added, by randomly drawing from a uniform distribution (between -0.1 and 0.1), small deviations to each proportion so that each row summed to less than one. The difference from one yielded a seventh unsampled source. Using this approach, we created two versions of synthetic datasets by varying the sampling seed and the magnitude of variation to create the unsampled source.

In each dataset, two matrices were created: one for the chemical tracers (used to create the chemical signatures in data stream 1), and another for eDNA metabarcoding (as input data stream 2). In dataset 1, both mixing proportion matrices were made very similar, mimicking an idealised scenario in which information coming from eDNA metabarcoding would reliably match the deposition and mixing process of chemical tracers. In dataset 2, the mixing proportion matrices differed substantially, most likely representing a realistic diversion between the two matrices. Their respective degrees of divergence can be seen in @fig-3. The mixing proportion matrix for chemical tracers was made identical between both datasets (@fig-2 a). All mixing proportion matrices used to simulate the two datasets were retained as "point of truth" to later evaluate the model performance---the closer the estimates are to the originally simulated mixing proportions, the better the model performance. The code pipeline used to create the synthetic datasets is part of the MixMustR package and can be accessed on GitHub (https://github.com/open-AIMS/MixMustR/blob/main/R/internal_data.R). The datasets are also provided as csv files in the online supplementary information.

As a benchmark, we tested how one of MixMustR models performed using both the synthetic datasets explained above (eight tracers, six fatty acids plus two stable isotopes). We chose the model variant that most closely resembles the structure of a MixSIAR model with a process error (Fig \ref{fig-1} c), and allows for a hierarchical component (Fig \ref{fig-1} e). For simplicity, we chose to keep the unsampled source tracer signatures fixed based on the mean across the tracers' signatures from the sampled sources (Fig \ref{fig-1} d). Results from all model variants across both synthetic datasets are available through the online supplementary information. The eDNA metabarcoding matrix (data stream 2) was transformed to the natural log scale to yield the input $\text{ln}\rho$, though we assumed two degrees of confidence, or measurement error, in the eDNA metabarcoding information (i.e., $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ = 0.1 across all observations in synthetic dataset 1, and $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ = 1 across all observations in synthetic dataset 2). Model performances were evaluated on the basis of goodness-of-fit using the Bayesian *R^2^* [@gelman2019amstat]. The total run time (in minutes) for each of the model variants was also recorded, and can be seen in Table S2.
 
We also compared model estimates obtained using both MixMustR and MixSIAR [@stock2018]. We first reformatted our synthetic data (i.e., by removing the non-stable isotope tracers) to input it into MixSIAR, then ran the model after specifying the same fitting specs (code available at https://github.com/open-aims/MixMustR_paper), which included defining the error structure within MixSIAR (i.e., process error with multiplicative error). Although we endeavoured to make comparisons as close as possible, MixMustR and MixSIAR have fundamental differences in several respects. For example, in MixSIAR the prior can only be cast on the global mean across the group-level means. These are priors on the concentration $\alpha$ vector of the Dirichlet distribution. We provided priors for $\alpha$ by taking the mean across group means from our eDNA metabarcoding dataset, and we then scaled the priors ($alpha_j = alpha_j \times J / \sum{alpha}$) following recommended practice [@stock2018]. Other important differences between the models include the underlying MCMC algorithms for computation (JAGS used Gibbs sampling, whereas Stan uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with No-U-Turn Sampling (HMC with NUTS)), the error structures are different, and the estimations of an unsampled source is not available in MixSIAR.

# Results and Discussion

\noindent The MixMustR model recovered the original mixing proportions well in idealised Dataset 1---the one in which the underlying mixing proportions from chemical tracers (data stream 1) and eDNA metabarcoding (data stream 2) were similar (mean Bayesian *R^2^* across sources: `{r} (tbl_1[1:7, ]) |> dplyr::filter(Source != "Unsampled") |> dplyr::pull(Mean) |> range() |> paste0(collapse = "\\textendash")`), when compared to Dataset 2---the one in which mixing proportions diverge (mean Bayesian *R^2^*: `{r} (tbl_1[8:14, ]) |> dplyr::filter(Source != "Unsampled") |> dplyr::pull(Mean) |> range() |> paste0(collapse = "\\textendash")`; @tbl-1). Equally unsurprising was the fact that the estimated mixing proportions were closer to the underlying mixing proportions from data stream 2 of Dataset 1 (yellow squares in @fig-4 a, Fig S1--4). This is expected given that we assigned a high degree of confidence ($\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ = 0.1) in the measurement error of the eDNA metabarcoding (data stream 2) mixing proportions. In general, all model variants performed poorly (i.e., a smaller *R^2^*) in recovering the originally simulated mixing proportion from the unsampled source in Dataset 2 (Fig S5--8). This is likely due to the divergence of the underlying mixing proportions, and the less confident measurement error of the eDNA metabarcoding mixing proportions ($\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ = 1). Inspections of posterior distributions and chain mixing also indicated acceptable fitting convergence for most models (Fig S9--24), though models fit to Dataset 2 required much more fine tuning of fitting specifications, such as longer chains and shorter steps, and a few did not converge (Fig S11, S18 and S23).

\noindent \underline{\textit{Comparison against MixSIAR}}

In terms of recovering the original mixing proportions from the sampled sources, there was a visible difference in estimates obtained by MixSIAR (@fig-5, @tbl-1) when compared to MixMustR (@fig-4, @tbl-1). Even in our analysis of Dataset 2, in which the underlying mixing proportions between data streams diverged, and the measurement error of data stream 2 was high, the overall performance (judging by R^2^ values) of MixMustR was still higher. That said, MixSIAR potentially captured the existence of at least one unsampled source judging by the posterior distribution of the multiplicative error term (parameter $\xi$ in ref. [@stock2018]), which included values much larger than 1, though with a high degree of uncertainty (mean = 0.93, 95% HDI: 0.35--2.00).

\noindent \underline{\textit{Assumptions and limitations of MixMustR}}

The basic formulation of most mixture models assumes that tracers are conserved through the mixing process [@stock2018], and MixMustR is not different in that respect. In simulating our test datasets, we envisaged a single soil sample taken from the surface, where there is assumed to be little to no diagenesis effects. If, however, practitioners wished to include down-core samples, then fractional adjustments for shifts in isotope ratios due to diagenesis and historical changes in atmospheric carbon signatures would need to be applied [@kruger2024]. The canonical usage of $\delta$^13^C and $\delta$^15^N is ideal in many cases because isotopic signatures may be corrected with diagenesis rates prior to the model. This type of correction is currently allowed in MixSIAR, for example, through the incorporation of a discrimination factor. Future versions of MixMustR could evolve to also include that flexibility. Overall, researchers are advised to carefully choose durable chemical tracers for the mixture analysis. For example, fatty acids are often used as a suite of biomarkers indicative of diverse sources in the diet of consumers [@derrien2017waterres]. However, fresh/living samples can often have very different proportions of lipids to decayed tissue due to some compounds (e.g., PUFAs) being rapidly broken-down and undetectable in soil or water samples (e.g., refs. [@kelly2012; @erlania2024ecolind]). Protocols for identifying tracers that are robust to environmental and ecological modification may be used to improve confidence in assigning contributions of different organic sources [@neubauer2015].

By allowing unknown sources to contribute to mixtures, MixMustR partially relaxes the common tenet that basic mixture models comprise all sources contributing to the mixture. Yet, it is important to recognise that this is only a strength insofar as the researcher has access to a high-quality second data stream to obtain an estimate of the "unsampled" sources that are lacking a chemical signature. We proposed information from eDNA metabarcoding could provide the second data stream but this dataset requires a carefully considered sampling and analysis pipeline to obtain an estimate of reads per amplicon sequence variant (ASV), which are then assigned to the target groups of interest (e.g., in blue carbon research those would be primary producers capable of fixing organic carbon via photosynthesis [@reef2017aslo; @ortega2020aslo; @erlania2023scitot]). These would be then classified into the sampled target source groups (i.e., the sampled sources), with all eDNA-derived ASVs that did not align with a primary producer, or could not be identified from DNA databases, might then combined into an extra unsampled group (Fig S25). Some of these unsampled ASVs may not be identifiable based on the available information in the taxonomic classifier database, and will therefore fall into a group called "unassigned". The success of this strategy depends on some key assumptions, particularly around the relative detection of different groups of interest, which is linked in some part to relative rates of shedding of decay [@beng2020biodiv]. Much more experimental work is needed to estimate these rates, and how they may affect the original mixing contribution and/or ASV-to-carbon ratios (*sensu* lipid tracers experiment [@erlania2024ecolind]). For these reasons, we simulated two different matching degrees between chemical tracers and mixing proportions as yielded from eDNA metabarcoding (see Methods for details) to test the robustness of MixMustR to tolerate some discrepancies in the proportions indicated by eDNA metabarcoding and the first data stream.

Choosing the appropriate value for the uncertainty around data stream 2, $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$, is not trivial. Therefore, the MixMustR package offers a simple tool which plots the expected variability in mixing proportion as a function of an input vector of mixing proportions from data stream 2 (one from each source), and their respective degrees of confidence or measurement error. Although the function does not inform the user what the expected uncertainty for each source and observation should be (which has to come from expert knowledge), it does allow the user to fine tune $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ until the appropriate variability in input mixing proportions is achieved. As an example, we show the expected variability in mixing proportions that would result from the values of $\sigma_{\text{ln}\rho}$ used to fit Datasets 1 and 2 (@fig-6). In determining a starting level of uncertainty to apply, researchers could use the proportion of reads among the unassigned ASVs in an eDNA metabarcoding dataset as a measure of uncertainty around the distribution in the proportion of reads per source group of interest. This is because those unassigned ASVs, which currently have no known Linnean classification or other form of TaxID using BLAST against the NCBI Taxonomy, could later be found to occupy one of the other assigned groups used to calculate estimated proportional occurrence once more becomes known about the genetic biodiversity present in a location.

MixMustR adds to the toolkit of ecologists and biogeochemists who may have access to multiple lines of evidence to back trace the most likely mixing proportions of their observed mixture. By evaluating MixMustR performance using a synthetic dataset of known composition we obtained insight into the underlying issues that influence estimates of source contributions to mixtures (in tune with previous work, e.g., ref. [@neubauer2015]). For example, as we observed from our results (@tbl-1, @fig-4, @fig-6), choosing the appropriate measurement error can have a large effect on model estimates and their associated uncertainty. In the idealised situation where a pipeline of data generation for data stream 2 matches the mixture process of chemical tracers in data stream 1 (similar to our synthetic Dataset 1), all MixMustR models will perform extremely well. If underlying mixing proportions do not match, then the models are likely to offer poorer performance. Thus, MixMustR offers researchers the ability to target investigations into differences in mixing proportions from data stream 1 and 2. In fact, we hope that MixMustR will spur research into innovative ways to conceive a second data stream. For example, in a blue carbon setting, alternative predictions for proportional contributions could be obtained from source-sink network models based on hydrodynamic-informed particle tracking to infer likely transport and deposition rates (e.g., ref. [@simpkins2025aslo]), or the relative proportion of probable sources from spatial habitat models of the target seascape (e.g., ref. [@asplund2021landecol]).

# Conclusion

\noindent The infinite mixture issue is long standing. MixMustR builds on a series of advances in this field, and it is inspired by emerging technologies and datasets which contribute to mixture modelling solutions. In leveraging information from independent lines of evidence, MixMustR takes us one step closer to uncovering mixing proportions in organic mixtures. Getting those mixtures right has taken unprecedented importance in understanding trophic pathways and understanding ecological functions. Moreover, identifying appropriate blue carbon sources can form the basis of policy development to conserve and enhance carbon sequestration with a mind to mitigating the increasing effects of climate change.
